newsitem.title: GERMANY: Parliament committee kills off German tax reform.
newsitem.headline: Parliament committee kills off German tax reform.

text.p: Germany's parliamentary mediation committee voted early on Thursday to reject sweeping government tax reforms, leaving virtually no chance they can become law before general elections next year.

The opposition majority on the committee -- a last-ditch forum for clearing legislative roadblocks -- voted after talks lasting 15 hours to kill off Finance Minister Theo Waigel's 30 billion mark ($16.3 billion) tax-cutting package.

Preliminary negotiations this week had found no basis for a tax deal between Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and the vote sent the plan back to the Bundestag lower house.
"We had to oppose the tax reform because it was not solidly financed," SPD tax negotiator Henning Voscherau, the mayor of Hamburg, told reporters after the marathon talks.
In the event, virtually the whole committee session was devoted to trying to end a two-year row over scrapping a five billion mark capital trading tax on companies.

Committee chairman Heribert Blens, of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), said a deal was reached to compensate local governments for lost revenues after the tax was dropped from the start of next year.

He said the agreement ensured that the capital trading tax would not have to be introduced in depressed eastern Germany, as would have otherwise been required under a ruling by the country's constitutional court.

This face-saving compromise did little to hide the massive differences over the fundamental approach to tax reforms, seen as urgently needed to help to increase investment and cut record post-war unemployment.
"I would have wished that this capacity to agree had been present over the great tax reform -- then we would have made a big leap forward," Waigel said before the talks ended.

The Bundestag will interrupt its summer recess to debate the tax reform next Tuesday. Waigel said he did not rule out forcing a second round of mediation to keep tax reforms at the top of the political agenda.

SPD chief whip Peter Struck said this would not change his party's opposition before general elections due in September 1998. "We have to expect that there will be no tax reform before 1998," he said earlier.
The opposition majority in the mediation committee also backed SPD proposals to cut the cost of employing workers by slashing occupational insurance charges from this October.

The SPD plan would cut unemployment and pensions insurance charges by one percentage point each, with the cost to be covered by a one-point hike in value-added tax, 10 pfennigs more tax on a litre of petrol and 2.5 pfennigs on heating oil.

But, just as the SPD voted down the government's tax reform with its majority in the Bundesrat upper house earlier this month, so the government will wield its Bundestag majority to kill off the SPD's scheme to cut payroll costs.
Rolf Peffekoven, a member of the 'five wise men' panel of independent government economic advisors, called the failure of the tax reform "a bitter setback for Germany".

"Top tax rates would have had to be cut to restore our country's competitiveness," he told Radio Bremen television. "The concept was definitely right, even if the financing had not been thought through properly."
Gerhard Grebe, economist at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt, told Reuters the cost of the failure of the tax reform could be half a percentage point in growth per year in the longer term.

"We are stuck in a reform logjam and now all important reforms will be postponed until after the elections," he said. "The tax reform would have been a signal abroad we could reform the system. Now I expect more firms to move jobs abroad."
